title: Payment service slow responses
executive_summary: INC-003 (SEV2): payment-service latency was elevated from about 18:10Z, with p95 rising from ~150ms to a window mean of ~1400ms and timeout rate rising from 0.1% to a mean of 2.9% (met-payment-service-p95_latency_ms-1750-1830, met-payment-service-timeout_rate-1750-1830). Payment CPU and error rate stayed flat, which is why pods looked healthy. The investigation status is ROOT_CAUSE_IDENTIFIED with confidence 0.73. The most probable explanation is upstream dependency degradation in auth-service: slow identity-provider JWKS refresh (first WARN 18:06:12Z, logpat-auth-service-171612d3) and request queueing on /v1/token/verify (first WARN 18:07:11Z, logpat-auth-service-9246cbf2) raised auth-service p95/p99 from 18:07Z (met-auth-service-p95_latency_ms-1750-1830) and auth error rate from 18:08Z (met-auth-service-error_rate-1750-1830). Payment calls to auth then slowed (WARN from 18:09:13Z, logpat-payment-service-4cb3914c) and began timing out at 3000ms (ERROR from 18:10:19Z, logpat-payment-service-4672e5cc). This is the most probable explanation, not a confirmed fact. Two gaps remain: identity-provider metrics could not be queried, and the 3000ms timeouts are not fully explained by auth server-side latency (auth max p95 was 2653ms).

critic_review.summary: H1 (auth-service latency degradation tied to slow identity-provider JWKS refresh, propagating to payment-service timeouts) is the leading hypothesis and is consistent in time: slow JWKS refresh WARN first at 18:06:12Z, auth queue-time WARN at 18:07:11Z, auth p95/p99 onset 18:07Z, auth error rate onset 18:08Z, payment slow-call WARN 18:09:13Z, payment p95 onset 18:09Z, payment timeout onset 18:10Z. Alternatives are contradicted: H2 (auth CPU saturation) fails because auth request_rate is flat (890 -> 905 rps, +1.6%, no onset) and auth CPU only rises at 18:10, three minutes after latency onset. H3 (payment DEBUG logging) fails because payment p95 was flat (~150ms) for 30+ minutes after the 17:35Z change, payment CPU is flat, and a DEBUG-keyword log search for payment in 17:35-18:12 returned no records. Postgres and redis latency are flat, and the payment CPU is flat, consistent with waiting on a dependency.  Caveats: auth's own timeout rate is unchanged and auth max p95 (2653ms) is below the 3000ms payment timeout, so the 3000ms timeouts are not fully explained by server-side auth latency; client-side queueing/retries on the payment->auth path are unverified. identity-provider metrics cannot be queried with the available tools (unknown service), so the JWKS slowness is supported only by auth logs. Postgres report_rollup slow statements (18:01-18:07Z) are an unexamined side signal; postgres p95 is flat and it is not on the auth path, so it is not ruled in.

assessments.reasoning: Timing is consistent: the earliest anomaly is the slow JWKS refresh at 18:06:12Z, followed by auth queueing, auth latency, auth errors, payment slow calls, and payment timeouts in order. Auth latency and error metrics, auth and payment logs, and flat postgres/redis/payment CPU all support it. Unresolved: identity-provider metrics are unobservable, and the 3000ms payment timeouts exceed auth's max server-side p95, so client-side or network queueing is unverified.

Auth request rate is flat (+1.6%, no onset), so there is no load increase. CPU onset is 18:10Z, after latency onset at 18:07Z, so CPU cannot be the initiating cause. CPU is better read as a symptom of the queueing.

Payment p95 was flat around 150ms from 17:40 to 18:05, about 30 minutes after the 17:35Z log-level change. Payment CPU is flat, and no DEBUG-level payment log records appear in 17:35-18:12Z. The change is temporally distant from the onset and has no mechanistic signature in the metrics or logs.

root_cause_statement: ROOT CAUSE IDENTIFIED (critic-approved; still an INFERENCE from evidence): upstream_dependency_degradation in auth-service - auth-service latency/queueing degradation on /v1/token/verify (likely tied to slow identity-provider JWKS refresh) propagates to payment-service, whose calls to auth time out at 3000ms.
corrective_actions: Mitigate the auth-service /v1/token/verify queueing: scale auth-service replicas or shed non-critical verify traffic while latency is elevated (met-auth-service-p95_latency_ms-1750-1830).

Investigate and restore identity-provider JWKS refresh performance (logpat-auth-service-171612d3); consider extending the cached JWKS TTL or serving the last-known-good key set during refresh slowness.
Review payment-service auth-call timeout and retry behavior so that client-side queueing/retries do not amplify latency on the payment->auth path (unverified per critic).
preventive_actions: Add bounded concurrency and queue-depth limits to auth-service token verification so queueing fails fast instead of accumulating multi-second waits.
Make JWKS refresh asynchronous with a background refresh and stale-while-revalidate behavior so a slow identity provider does not block request paths.
Add identity-provider as a monitored service so its latency and error metrics can be queried during future incidents (evidence gap: 'unknown service identity-provider').
Set payment-service auth timeouts and circuit breaking with a fallback or fast-fail policy, and document the dependency timeout budget.
monitoring_recommendations: Alert on auth-service p95 and p99 latency for /v1/token/verify (baseline ~45ms / ~90ms; onset observed at 18:07Z).
Alert on the auth-service 'Request queue time high' and 'Slow JWKS refresh' WARN log patterns, with a threshold on frequency per minute.
Alert on payment-service timeout_rate and on the 'Call to auth-service took' WARN pattern (onset 18:09Z, timeout onset 18:10Z).
Track payment-service p95 latency separately from CPU and error rate, since CPU and errors did not reflect this degradation.
Monitor the Postgres report_rollup slow statements (18:01-18:07Z) as an unexamined side signal.
limitations: 1 tool calls failed and 0 returned partial data; affected areas are treated as unknown, not healthy.
Confidence values are rule-based evidence-strength scores, not calibrated probabilities.
Investigation terminated because: critic verdict APPROVED
conclusion: The most probable root cause is auth-service latency and queueing on /v1/token/verify, likely tied to slow identity-provider JWKS refresh, which propagated to payment-service as call slowness and 3000ms timeouts. Auth CPU saturation (H2) and payment DEBUG logging (H3) were rejected. Postgres and Redis were flat and are not implicated on the auth path. Confidence is 0.73 because identity-provider metrics were unavailable and the 3000ms timeouts are not fully explained by server-side auth latency. Closing these gaps should be the next step.
